title: Gerhard: venial/mortal labels track mercy and person, not the act’s nature—with four cautions
source_text: LV. Qua de re tota prolixe agit Joannes Gerhardus in locis Theologicis, ubi circa hanc distinctionem mentem suam explicat his verbis. Quod peccata quaedam dicuntur venialia, quaedam tantum mortalia, id non fit propter naturam peccatorum, sed propter misericordiam Patris, meritum Filii, & sanctificationem Spiritus; ac respicit haec divisio non omnes homines in genere, sed tantum renatos; nec desumenda est ex lege, quae omnia peccata qualiacunque & quantulacunque sint, accusat & damnat; sed ex Evan-gelio, quod ostendit credentibus in Christum peccata infirmitatis, ignorantiae, & pravas concupiscentias non imputari, si eis resistant, hoc est, si renati 1. Haec mala in corde habitantia agnoscant: 2. De illis serio doleant: 3. Merito Mediatoris velut umbra-culo tegi petant & credant: 4. Frena eis nequaquam laxent, sed Spiritu eis resistant, crucifigentes carnem cum concupiscentiis. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, 1. In non re-natis nulla esse peccata venialia, sed omnia mortalia: 2. Venialia peccata esse talia non ex natura ipsius actus, sed ex conditione personae delinquentis, quae si est in Christo per fidem, peccata infirmitatis teguntur: 3. Nomen mortalis peccati non esse satis commodum, dicendum potius erat mortiferum ac regnans: 4. Nec venialium pecca-torum nomen satis commodum est, dicenda potius erant peccata infirmitatis, lapsus hu-mani, pravae concupiscentiae, &c. Neque enim ideo dicuntur venialia, quod in se & ex se venia sint digna; sed quod Deus credentibus ea dimittere veniaque dignetur. Tom. 2, tract. 13. de Peccatis actualibus, cap. 19, num. 92.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning this whole matter John Gerhard treats at length in his Theological Commonplaces, where around this distinction he explains his mind in these words. That certain sins are called venial, certain only mortal, happens not because of the nature of the sins but because of the Father’s mercy, the Son’s merit, and the Spirit’s sanctification; and this division regards not all men in general but only the regenerate; nor is it to be drawn from the law, which accuses and condemns all sins of whatever kind and howsoever small; but from the Gospel, which shows that to believers in Christ sins of infirmity, of ignorance, and depraved concupiscences are not imputed if they resist them—that is, if the regenerate (1) acknowledge these evils dwelling in the heart; (2) seriously grieve over them; (3) ask and believe to be covered by the Mediator’s merit as by a shade; (4) by no means give them rein but resist them by the Spirit, crucifying the flesh with its lusts. From all which it appears: (1) in the unregenerate there are no venial sins, but all are mortal; (2) venial sins are such not from the nature of the act itself but from the condition of the delinquent person, who if in Christ by faith has infirmity-sins covered; (3) the name ‘mortal sin’ is not convenient enough—it should rather have been said mortiferous and reigning; (4) nor is the name of venial sins convenient enough—they should rather have been called sins of infirmity, human falls, depraved concupiscence, etc. For they are not called venial because in and of themselves they are worthy of pardon; but because God deigns to forgive and pardon them to believers. Tom. 2, tract. 13, on Actual Sins, ch. 19, no. 92.
pass_b_english: Gerhard: ‘venial/mortal’ labels track Trinitarian mercy toward the regenerate, not the act’s nature under law.
Four marks of resisting infirmity, then four cautions—prefer ‘mortiferous/reigning’ and ‘infirmity-falls’ over the Roman names.

choices.english: not from the nature of the act itself
